patients.summary: Former construction laborer on disability with severe alcohol use disorder who joins in 2021 with hypertension and peptic ulcer disease, is found to have alcoholic cirrhosis in 2023, and decompensates with ascites, encephalopathy and variceal bleeding through 2026, ending with a TIPS and an open transplant evaluation.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
NEW PATIENT

50 y/o man here to establish. Previous PCP office no longer took his insurance; he has been stretching his BP pills. Wife waited in the car.

HTN: told he had high pressure around 2016, on amlodipine 5 since. Does not check at home. No headaches, chest pain, dyspnea.

Ulcer history: had an ulcer around 2017 at the old office, treated, has stayed on pantoprazole daily since. No current heartburn, no black stools, no vomiting.

Alcohol: drinks beer every day, usually a six-pack, has for about 13 years, more on weekends. Has had stretches of cutting back that do not last. No withdrawal seizures or DTs he knows of. Has never been in a program. Not interested in a referral today, said he would try to cut down on his own.

Tobacco: about two-thirds of a pack a day since his early twenties. Tried quitting once with gum.

Work: laborer on building crews for most of his life; out on disability leave now.

Family: father drank heavily and died of liver cirrhosis at 58. Mother has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. A brother also struggles with alcohol.

Meds: amlodipine 5 mg daily, pantoprazole 40 mg daily.
Allergies: none known.

ROS otherwise negative.

Exam: BP 142/90 seated, repeated similar. Well appearing, a little ruddy. Sclerae white. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear, no wheeze. Abdomen soft, nontender, no mass felt, no distension. No edema. Gait steady.

AUDIT-C 10. PHQ-2 1.

A/P
1. Hypertension, above goal on amlodipine 5. Away from meds on and off; refilled, recheck in a few months before changing anything.
2. Peptic ulcer disease, history - continue pantoprazole.
3. Alcohol use disorder, severe by history. Talked plainly about his dad's liver and what daily use does. He wants to try cutting down first. Gave the program list; door is open.
4. Tobacco - advised to quit, he will think about it; offered patch or other aids.
5. Health maintenance - Tdap today. Fasting labs ordered. Records request for old practice. Colon screening: says he did a stool card last year, will confirm with records.

Return 3-4 months.

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
ANNUAL PHYSICAL

52 y/o man for yearly exam; rescheduled from last month. Fasting labs drawn this AM, finally.

Interval: no ER visits. BP meds daily. Beer most days, about six. Smoking 2/3 ppd, figures 20 pack-years give or take. Sleeping ok. Mood fine, PHQ-9 3. Wife is after him to cut back.

ROS: no chest pain, no shortness of breath, no abdominal pain, no blood in stool, no vomiting blood, no swelling.

Meds: amlodipine 5 daily, pantoprazole 40 daily. NKDA.

Exam: BP 138/88. Alert, conversant. Eyes anicteric. Oropharynx clear. Neck supple, no nodes. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender, no organ enlargement appreciated, no fluid. Skin without rash. No edema. Neuro grossly normal.

A/P
- Preventive: flu and first Shingrix today. Lung screening CT ordered - meets criteria with his pack-years. FIT due next month; kit at front desk.
- HCV and HIV screening sent with today's labs.
- HTN: acceptable, continue amlodipine.
- Alcohol: same conversation, same answer. Will look at the liver tests with him.
- Tobacco: advised to stop.

See results note.

documents.title: Physical lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Scott - your labs are back. Kidney function, sugar and cholesterol are fine, and the hepatitis C and HIV tests are negative. Two things stand out: your liver enzymes are up (AST 76, ALT 52) and your platelet count is a little low at 138. That pattern fits with daily drinking stressing the liver. The best treatment is cutting way back or stopping. I would like to repeat these in about 3 months - the lab order is in. If you want help with the drinking, the program list I gave you still stands, or call me.

LOW-DOSE CT CHEST, LUNG CANCER SCREENING (BASELINE)
Indication: 52-year-old current smoker, approximately 20 pack-years.
Technique: Low-dose helical CT of the chest without contrast.
Findings: Lungs are clear without nodule, mass or consolidation. No emphysema. Airways patent. No pleural effusion. Heart size normal, no pericardial effusion. No mediastinal or hilar adenopathy. Visualized upper abdomen unremarkable. No acute osseous abnormality.
reports.conclusion: Lung-RADS 1: negative. Continue annual screening in 12 months.

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: abdomen getting bigger.

HPI: Over about two months his belly has been steadily swelling, with a tight, uncomfortable feeling, worse after he eats. His appetite has dropped off and he has lost about ten pounds over the same stretch even though his pants are tighter. No vomiting, no blood in vomit, no black or bloody stools, no fever. Has not had a drink in roughly a month - says the swelling scared him and his wife "put her foot down." Before that, about six beers a day going back fifteen years. Still smoking.

Meds: amlodipine 5, pantoprazole 40. NKDA.

Exam: afebrile, vitals stable, BP 128/80, weight 80 kg (85 last fall). Not jaundiced to my eye in office lighting. Several spider angiomas over the upper chest and shoulders. Palms red at the thenar and hypothenar eminences. Abdomen protuberant, nontender; flank dullness that moves when he rolls to his side, and a fluid wave is present. Liver edge not clearly felt through the fluid. Trace ankle edema at most. No asterixis. Oriented, conversant.

Impression: new ascites with stigmata of chronic liver disease in a man with long, heavy alcohol use and liver enzymes that were already up last fall. Cirrhosis is the leading concern until shown otherwise.

Plan:
- CMP, CBC, PT/INR drawn today, before he left.
- Abdominal ultrasound with portal vein duplex, requested this week.
- Come back Friday for results; sooner and to the ED for confusion, fever, belly pain, vomiting blood or black stools.
- Stay off alcohol completely. Low salt in the meantime.
- Talked with him and his wife in the room about what this likely means. He was quiet, asked good questions.

reports.text:
ULTRASOUND ABDOMEN COMPLETE WITH DUPLEX OF THE PORTAL VENOUS SYSTEM
Indication: Ascites on exam; abnormal liver tests; heavy alcohol use.
Findings:
Liver: Coarsened echotexture with nodular surface contour, consistent with cirrhosis. No focal hepatic lesion identified.
Portal vein: Patent with hepatopetal flow. No thrombus.
Hepatic veins: Patent.
Gallbladder: No stones. No wall thickening. No pericholecystic fluid.
Bile ducts: Not dilated. Common duct 4 mm.
Spleen: Enlarged, 14.8 cm in length.
Pancreas: Visualized portions unremarkable.
Kidneys: Normal size and echogenicity bilaterally. No hydronephrosis.
Aorta: Normal caliber.
Ascites: Moderate free fluid in all four quadrants.
reports.conclusion:
1. Cirrhotic liver morphology without focal lesion.
2. Splenomegaly.
3. Ascites.
4. Patent portal vein; no portal vein thrombosis.

documents.title: Results Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Results visit, wife present.

Labs 6/27: Hgb 12.5, plt 110 (was 138 last fall), INR 1.3, T bili 2.8, albumin 3.2, AST 120, ALT 90, alk phos 110. Kidney function and electrolytes ok.
Ultrasound 6/29: nodular cirrhotic liver without a mass, enlarged spleen, ascites, portal vein open with normal-direction flow.

No drinking since late May, he says. Belly unchanged since Tuesday.

Assessment: Alcoholic cirrhosis with ascites and portal hypertension (splenomegaly, low platelets). Low albumin. Spider angiomas on exam. This is decompensated by the presence of fluid.

Plan:
1. Spironolactone 100 mg + furosemide 40 mg each morning. Sodium under 2 g/day - handout reviewed. Daily weights; call if down more than about 1 kg/day, dizzy, or cramping badly.
2. BMP in about 10 days with a visit.
3. GI referral for liver care and an upper scope to look for varices. Earliest new slot with the group is in January; asked to be put on the cancellation list.
4. Alcohol: he says he is done. Referral to outpatient program placed today and he agreed - big step. Wife will drive.
5. Hepatitis B/C serologies drawn; will vaccinate against hep A/B if not immune.
6. No NSAIDs. Tylenol up to 2 g/day max.
7. Smoking: he wants to quit too, picked July 1 as a date.

Return in 2-3 weeks. ED for fever, belly pain, confusion, vomiting blood or black stool.

documents.title: Hepatitis results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Scott, the hepatitis tests show no hepatitis B or C infection. You also do not have protection against hepatitis B (and we have no record of hepatitis A vaccination), so we will start both vaccines at your visit on the 18th. With a liver that is already scarred, it is worth protecting it.

documents.title: Follow-up Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
F/u ascites on diuretics.

Taking spironolactone and furosemide every morning, peeing a lot the first few days, now settled. Pants fit again. Some leg cramps at night, mild. No dizziness. Eating a bit better.

Alcohol: no drinks since late May. Did his intake at the outpatient program on the 10th; groups three evenings a week. AUDIT-C 0.
Tobacco: stopped July 1. Using hard candy and keeping busy. Proud of this, as he should be.

Exam: BP 124/78, wt 77 kg (80 on 6/27). Abdomen much softer, mild residual dullness in the flanks, no fluid wave. No edema. No asterixis.

BMP today - will review when back.

A/P
1. Alcoholic cirrhosis with ascites - responding. Same doses. Low sodium.
2. AUD - in early remission, in outpatient treatment. Encouraged.
3. Former smoker as of 7/1.
4. Hep A #1 and hep B #1 today; hep B #2 in a month, then both at 6 months.
5. GI still January; on cancellation list.

RTC 3 months with labs.

documents.title: Gastroenterology consultation and upper endoscopy (visit 2024-01-08)
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE GASTROENTEROLOGY - CLINIC LETTER
Date of service: 01/08/2024
Referred by: primary care, for alcohol-related cirrhosis with ascites

Thank you for sending Mr. Pomeroy, 53, whose cirrhosis came to light last summer when he presented with a distended abdomen. He tells me he has been abstinent for roughly six months and is attending an outpatient recovery program. He also gave up cigarettes in July. He has no complaints today aside from an intermittent mild burning in the upper abdomen that he calls indigestion. No melena, hematemesis or confusion.

PMH: hypertension; remote peptic ulcer; alcohol use disorder; cirrhosis with ascites, controlled on diuretics.
Meds: amlodipine 5 mg daily, pantoprazole 40 mg daily, spironolactone 100 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.
FH: father died at 58 of alcohol-related cirrhosis.

Exam: BP 140/90, HR 78, afebrile. No jaundice. Abdomen soft without ascites; spleen tip palpable, moderately enlarged; liver edge firm and palpable below the costal margin. No peripheral edema. No asterixis.

Labs today: platelets 110, AST 70, ALT 50, total bilirubin 1.2, albumin 3.9, INR 1.1.

Procedure (same day): Diagnostic esophagogastroduodenoscopy under moderate sedation. Small esophageal varices in the distal esophagus. No red wale markings. No stigmata of recent bleeding. Stomach and duodenum without ulcer.

Impression: Compensated-on-treatment alcoholic cirrhosis with portal hypertension; small esophageal varices meeting our threshold for primary prophylaxis.

Plan:
1. Start propranolol 20 mg twice daily; hold for pulse under 55 or dizziness.
2. Continue current diuretics and pantoprazole.
3. Liver ultrasound every 6 months for surveillance; we would appreciate the PCP ordering these locally.
4. Repeat endoscopy in about a year, sooner for any bleeding.
5. Total abstinence; he is doing very well.

Sincerely,
Gastroenterology

documents.author: PCP

Cirrhosis f/u. GI letter (1/8 visit) finally reached us in February - reviewed: small varices on scope, no red signs, propranolol 20 BID started; ultrasound q6 months asked of us.

Now ~10.5 months without alcohol, still in recovery group weekly. No smoking. Tolerating propranolol; a bit less stamina climbing stairs, otherwise fine. No bleeding, no dark stools, no confusion. Belly stays flat on the diuretics. The indigestion GI mentioned comes and goes, mild, no change in pattern.

Meds reconciled: amlodipine 5, pantoprazole 40, spironolactone 100, furosemide 40, propranolol 20 BID.

Exam: BP 126/80, HR 64. Wt 78. Anicteric. Spider angiomas on the chest. Abdomen soft, no shifting dullness, spleen tip felt. No edema. No asterixis.

A/P
1. Alcoholic cirrhosis with portal HTN - stable, ascites controlled. Labs today.
2. Esophageal varices on primary prophylaxis - HR at a sensible target.
3. AUD, early remission - continuing.
4. HCC surveillance US ordered for July.
5. Peptic ulcer history - on pantoprazole.

RTC 4-5 months.

documents.title: Hospital discharge summary (admitted 2024-09-10, discharged 2024-09-14)
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
REGIONAL HOSPITAL - DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admission: 09/10/2024   Discharge: 09/14/2024
Service: Hospital Medicine

Principal diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy.
Secondary: Alcoholic cirrhosis with recurrent ascites; portal hypertension; esophageal varices on beta-blocker; alcohol use disorder with recent relapse; hypertension.

History: 53-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis brought by his wife after several days of daytime somnolence, word-finding trouble and increasing abdominal girth. Resumed drinking about a month before admission after roughly 14 months of abstinence.

Course: On arrival drowsy but arousable, with asterixis and ascites. Infectious evaluation unrevealing. No GI bleeding. Started on lactulose with rapid improvement; mental status at baseline by hospital day 3. Diuretics continued. Alcohol withdrawal monitored without significant symptoms. Social work met with patient and wife regarding return to outpatient treatment.

Discharge medications:
- Lactulose 30 mL by mouth twice daily, adjust to 2-3 soft bowel movements a day (NEW)
- Spironolactone 100 mg daily
- Furosemide 40 mg daily
- Propranolol 20 mg twice daily
- Pantoprazole 40 mg daily
- Amlodipine 5 mg daily
Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Follow-up: PCP within 1-2 weeks; gastroenterology as scheduled. No driving until cleared. Abstain from alcohol.

medications.sig: Take 30 mL by mouth twice daily; adjust to 2-3 soft bowel movements daily

procedures.procedure: Transitional care management, moderate complexity

documents.title: Post-Hospital Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
TCM visit, discharged 9/14. Summary received 9/20 and reviewed. Wife with him; RN reached them by phone 9/16 for the interactive contact.

Admitted 9/10-9/14 for hepatic encephalopathy with fluid back in the belly; infection workup negative; cleared quickly on lactulose.

Now: thinking clear per wife. On lactulose 30 mL twice a day, getting 2-3 soft BMs; she watches the count. Belly a bit fuller than spring. No bleeding.

Alcohol: honest about it - started again in August, a few beers most nights, more on weekends. Has had nothing since admission. Wants to go back to the program; already called them. AUDIT-C scored for the past year: 8.
Mood: down about the relapse, PHQ-9 6, no SI.

Meds reconciled; lactulose added to our list.

Exam: BP 124/78. Wt 80 (78 in April). Awake, oriented x3, conversant. No asterixis. Anicteric. Abdomen mildly distended with shifting dullness, nontender. Trace ankle edema.

A/P
1. Hepatic encephalopathy, first episode - resolved on lactulose. Continue; titrate to 2-3 BMs. No driving for now.
2. Ascites, recurrent with the relapse - same diuretics, strict low salt; weigh daily.
3. AUD with relapse - re-entering outpatient program. Talked about his father without lecturing. He knows.
4. Varices - propranolol continues; GI recheck scope is due around the new year.
5. Flu shot offered - he declined today, "too much going on."

Labs today. RTC 6-8 weeks, sooner if any confusion.

documents.title: Post-hospital labs
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Scott and Linda - labs from yesterday: bilirubin is back up to 2.4, albumin down to 3.1, liver enzymes higher (AST 110), sodium slightly low at 133, platelets 92. Kidney function is fine. This is the liver reacting to the drinking this summer, and much of it can improve again with sobriety, like last year. No medication changes. Please keep the salt low and the fluids reasonable.

documents.title: Gastroenterology follow-up and endoscopy with banding (visit 2024-12-31)
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE GASTROENTEROLOGY - FOLLOW-UP
Date of service: 12/31/2024

Mr. Pomeroy is a 54-year-old man with alcohol-associated cirrhosis and esophageal varices, here for his scheduled yearly visit and repeat endoscopy. About a week ago he brought up blood once; he thought it was from his old ulcer. Nothing since: no further vomiting, no change in his stools, no belly pain. He acknowledges ongoing drinking this fall; his most recent drink was two days ago. Hospitalized in September for encephalopathy.

Meds: propranolol 20 mg BID, lactulose 30 mL BID, spironolactone 100 mg, furosemide 40 mg, pantoprazole 40 mg, amlodipine 5 mg.
Allergies: none.

Exam: Vitals stable. Alert, no asterixis. Spleen mildly enlarged to palpation. No ascites detected. No caput medusae.

Labs: Hgb 12.5, platelets 90, INR 1.2, AST 70, ALT 30, alkaline phosphatase 100, albumin 3.2.

Procedure: EGD under monitored anesthesia care. Large varices in the lower third of the esophagus without active bleeding. Band ligation performed; four bands placed. No gastric varices. No ulcer in the stomach or duodenum.

Impression: Varices have progressed from small to large despite propranolol; the recent single episode of hematemesis is presumed variceal in origin.

Plan:
1. Continue propranolol 20 mg BID.
2. Repeat banding in about 4 weeks and then at intervals until the varices are eradicated.
3. Continue lactulose and diuretics.
4. Abstinence strongly advised; he is re-engaging with treatment.
5. Any further bleeding: emergency department immediately.

Gastroenterology

documents.title: Follow-up Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
F/u. Missed November. GI letter for 12/31 received mid-January: varices now large, banded, one episode of vomiting blood the week before. He tells me he had the second banding on 1/28 - no paperwork from that one; throat sore for two days, otherwise fine.

Alcohol: cut way down since the new year but "a few on Saturdays." Back at the program one evening a week. AUDIT-C 6. Wife says no confusion; lactulose 2-3 BMs/day.
No further hematemesis, no black stools.

Exam: BP 118/74, HR 62. Wt 79. Anicteric. Abdomen soft, mild flank dullness. Spider angiomas. No edema. No asterixis.

US 1/21: no lesion, small ascites.

A/P
1. Large esophageal varices, banding series underway with GI; propranolol continues; HR fine.
2. Cirrhosis with small ascites - diuretics same; BMP today.
3. HE on lactulose - no recurrence.
4. AUD - still drinking on weekends. Asked him to tell his GI team the same. We talked about the next bleed being the dangerous one.
5. Lung screening CT: he still does not want it this year. Order closed; will revisit in the fall.

RTC 2-3 months.

documents.title: He was in the hospital again
documents.author: patient
documents.body: This is Linda writing for Scott. He was in the hospital again from Tuesday to Saturday last week. Same thing as September, he got very confused and his stomach blew up. They drained a lot of fluid out. He is home and clearer now. They said to follow up with you. Can we get an appointment? Also they gave him new papers but nothing about his meds changed.

documents.title: RE: He was in the hospital again
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Thank you for letting us know, Linda. I booked him for Tuesday 4/22 at 1:40 with the doctor. Please bring the discharge papers. We have asked the hospital to fax the summary. If he gets confused again, has a fever, belly pain, or any blood in vomit or stool, go straight to the emergency room.

procedures.procedure: Transitional care management, high complexity

documents.title: Post-Hospital Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Post-hospital visit; discharge summary not yet received - working from the patient's papers and wife's account.

Admitted 4/8-4/12: confusion again with a tense belly; large-volume paracentesis; lactulose continued. Papers list the same medications as before.

Today: clear-headed, oriented. Admits the lactulose had slipped to once a day before the admission because it was inconvenient when out on errands. Back to twice daily now, 2-3 BMs. Drinking: admits weekend beers through March. Says he is done; skeptical look from his wife.

Exam: BP 116/72. Wt 77. Anicteric. Abdomen moderately soft, small amount of flank dullness, paracentesis site healed. No asterixis. No edema.

A/P
1. Recurrent hepatic encephalopathy - second admission. Lactulose BID, titrate to 2-3 BMs, not fewer. Wife to keep the BM count on the fridge.
2. Recurrent ascites - post-paracentesis; diuretics same, low salt.
3. Large varices - next banding per GI.
4. AUD - ongoing use; he says he wants to go back to more intensive sessions. Encouraged him to call the program this week.
5. Labs today. Request discharge summary again.

RTC 6 weeks.

documents.title: Post-hospital labs
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Labs yesterday: bilirubin 2.6, albumin 3.0, INR 1.4, platelets 84, hemoglobin 11.6, sodium 132. These are the weakest numbers your liver has shown, Scott. Kidneys are fine. This is the point where stopping drinking for good changes what happens next. No medication changes.

documents.body:
REGIONAL HOSPITAL - DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 04/08/2025  Discharged 04/12/2025

Diagnoses: Hepatic encephalopathy, recurrent. Tense ascites in alcohol-related cirrhosis. Esophageal varices, under banding. Alcohol use disorder.

Presentation: Brought in by wife for two days of confusion and sleepiness with a tight abdomen. Encephalopathic on arrival with asterixis. Tense ascites.

Course: Large-volume paracentesis on day 1 with albumin replacement; fluid without evidence of infection. Lactulose increased in hospital with clearing of mentation by day 3; home dosing resumed at discharge. No bleeding. Patient reported intermittent alcohol use; counseled.

Discharge medications (unchanged): lactulose 30 mL BID, spironolactone 100 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, propranolol 20 mg BID, pantoprazole 40 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.
Follow-up: PCP 1-2 weeks; GI for continued banding.

documents.title: No-show outreach
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Missed 10:20 appt. Called home and cell, left message on cell asking him to call back to reschedule and to confirm he is ok. Will try wife's number tomorrow if no call back.

documents.title: No-show outreach, follow-up
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Reached wife. He is home, not confused, taking his meds; overslept yesterday. Rebooked for August after his next ultrasound. She will call sooner if anything changes.

documents.body: Hi Doc. Wanted you to know I went back to the program full time the first week of July, 3 nights a week. Last beer was June 24. I'm doing it for real this time. See you in August.

documents.title: RE: Update
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Scott, this is the best message I have had all month. Thank you for telling me. Keep going to every session. See you in August - and call any time before then.

ANNUAL EXAM

55 y/o man. Sober since late June, four months now; still going to his program and meets his sponsor weekly. No cigarettes since 2023. Living at home with his wife; on disability.

No confusion episodes since April. No hematemesis or melena. A little more tired than he would like. Belly stable.

Meds: propranolol 20 BID, lactulose 30 mL BID, spironolactone 100, furosemide 40, pantoprazole 40, amlodipine 5. NKDA.

Exam: Vitals as recorded. Alert, oriented. Sclerae clear. Mouth and throat normal. Neck without nodes. Heart regular. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nondistended, spleen tip palpable. Spider angiomas upper chest. Palmar erythema. No edema. No asterixis. Neuro nonfocal.

PHQ-9 2, AUDIT-C 0.

A/P
- Alcoholic cirrhosis, portal hypertension, large varices with banding, HE and ascites history: stable on current regimen. Labs today.
- Prevention: flu and COVID done 10/7; Tdap 2021; PCV20 2021; Shingrix complete; hep A/B complete. Colon screening: FIT last done 2023 - kit given today. Lung CT due; he agrees this year - ordered.
- AUD in early remission.

RTC 3 months.

TCM visit. No records from the hospital yet; history from patient, wife and his discharge instructions sheet.

12/30: vomited a large volume of blood at home, wife drove him to the ED. Fluids, an urgent scope that showed bleeding esophageal varices - banded. Admitted, home 1/2. The sheet says GI follow-up for banding in about 3-4 weeks; no new medications listed.

Before this he had a few weeks of being more tired and filling up fast at meals.

Since home: no more blood, stools brown, appetite fair, tired. No confusion. Sober since 6/24 - six months now, still in his program. AUDIT-C 0.

Meds: propranolol 20 BID, lactulose 30 mL BID, spironolactone 100, furosemide 40, pantoprazole 40, amlodipine 5.

Exam: BP 110/70, HR 66. Wt 76. Pale conjunctivae. Anicteric. Spider angiomas. Abdomen soft, mild flank dullness, nontender. No asterixis.

1. Bleeding esophageal varices, s/p endoscopic banding 12/30. Continue propranolol; GI banding series to continue - he has 1/27.
2. Anemia from blood loss - CBC today.
3. Cirrhosis with ascites, HE - regimen unchanged.
4. AUD - six months sober. Real progress despite the bleed.

documents.body:
REGIONAL HOSPITAL EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT - PHYSICIAN RECORD
Date of visit: 12/30/2025

CC: vomiting blood.

HPI: 55-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis and known esophageal varices, brought in by his wife after a large-volume hematemesis at home this afternoon. Over the past several weeks he has felt progressively more fatigued, gets full early, and has had mild, intermittent abdominal discomfort. Prior admissions for ascites and hepatic encephalopathy.

PMH: alcoholic cirrhosis with portal hypertension; esophageal varices with prior band ligation; hypertension; peptic ulcer disease; recurrent hepatic encephalopathy; recurrent ascites; alcohol use disorder.
Meds: amlodipine 5 mg daily, propranolol 20 mg BID, lactulose 30 mL BID, pantoprazole 40 mg daily, spironolactone 100 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.
Social: former smoker, 20 pack-years. Alcohol use disorder, abstinent about 6 months, in an outpatient rehabilitation program. On disability, formerly a construction laborer.
FH: father with alcohol-related cirrhosis, died at 58; mother with hypertension and diabetes; sibling with alcohol use disorder.

Exam: Pale and diaphoretic. Abdomen distended with shifting dullness. Multiple spider angiomas across the chest. 

Labs: anemia and thrombocytopenia (see laboratory record).

ED course: Two large-bore IVs; crystalloid resuscitation with improvement. GI consulted. Bedside upper endoscopy after resuscitation: dilated veins of the distal esophagus with stigmata of recent hemorrhage; band ligation performed.

Impression: Acute variceal hemorrhage from esophageal varices due to portal hypertension.

Disposition: Admitted to the medical service with GI following.

documents.title: Hospital discharge summary (admitted 2026-06-30, discharged 2026-07-08)
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
REGIONAL HOSPITAL - DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted via ED 06/30/2026   Discharged 07/08/2026
Services: Medical ICU; Hepatology; Interventional Radiology

Principal diagnosis: Acute esophageal variceal hemorrhage with hypovolemic shock.
Secondary: Decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis with tense ascites and jaundice; portal hypertension; splenomegaly; thrombocytopenia; history of recurrent hepatic encephalopathy; hypertension; peptic ulcer disease; alcohol use disorder in sustained remission.

Presentation: Abrupt hematemesis at home with signs of hypovolemic shock on arrival. Background of jaundice, prior admissions for hepatic encephalopathy and upper GI bleeding. Endoscopic band ligation had failed to control his recurrent bleeding, and his nonselective beta-blocker had been discontinued because of bradycardia. On exam: tense ascites, scleral icterus, spider angiomata.

Home medications on admission (from prior records): amlodipine 5 mg daily, propranolol 20 mg BID, lactulose 30 mL BID, pantoprazole 40 mg daily, spironolactone 100 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily. Propranolol confirmed stopped in 03/2026; not resumed.

Labs: thrombocytopenia, elevated INR and low albumin.
Imaging: Abdominal ultrasound - shrunken liver, dilated portal vein, splenomegaly.

Hospital course: Resuscitated in the ED and admitted to the ICU. Packed red cells transfused. Octreotide infusion started for variceal hemorrhage. After stabilization, surgery and hepatology reviewed portosystemic shunt options for portal decompression; the consensus was a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt. Therapeutic paracentesis for tense ascites. TIPS placed by interventional radiology on 07/02/2026 via right internal jugular access without complication. No rebleeding after TIPS. Octreotide completed. Mental status monitored closely after TIPS; lactulose continued. Ambulating at discharge.

Discharge medications: lactulose 30 mL BID (titrate to 2-3 soft stools); spironolactone 100 mg daily; furosemide 40 mg daily; pantoprazole 40 mg daily; amlodipine 5 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.

Follow-up:
1. PCP within 1-2 weeks.
2. Post-TIPS duplex ultrasound in about 3 weeks (scheduled).
3. Referral to the liver transplant center for evaluation; decompensated cirrhosis with more than 12 months of abstinence documented by his treatment program will be needed.
4. Return for bleeding, confusion, fever or abdominal pain.

documents.title: Liver transplant center intake (visit 2026-08-18)
documents.author: transplant hepatology
documents.body:
LIVER TRANSPLANT PROGRAM - INITIAL EVALUATION VISIT
Date of service: 08/18/2026

Dear colleague,

We met Mr. Pomeroy, 55, and his wife today for an intake visit. He has alcohol-associated cirrhosis decompensated by recurrent ascites, recurrent hepatic encephalopathy and variceal hemorrhage, most recently a bleed with shock in late June treated with a TIPS on 07/02. He reports abstinence since late June 2025 with ongoing participation in an outpatient program, and a former smoking history of 20 pack-years with none since 2023.

We reviewed the hospital records, your notes and the post-TIPS ultrasound.

Assessment: Appropriate to begin formal transplant evaluation.

Plan:
1. Our coordinator will schedule the evaluation testing and consultations at the center.
2. Please continue to support his recovery; we will request a letter from his treatment program and will monitor abstinence as part of evaluation.
3. Continue his current medications and your routine primary care.

We will keep you informed.

Transplant Hepatology
